l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L20: Cloud technology.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Define cloud computing and give examples of cloud services. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Cloud computing means using computing resources, such as storage space and software, that are delivered on demand over the internet from remote servers. Instead of keeping files and programs on their own hard drives, organisations and individuals keep them on servers in large data centres owned by cloud providers. They can then reach them from any device with an internet connection. Familiar examples include OneDrive, Google Drive, iCloud and Microsoft 365.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Organisations usually pay a monthly subscription or use a pay-as-you-go plan. The cloud is growing quickly because it is flexible: a business can start small and add more storage or users when it needs them. It has also changed everyday life for young people, from saving coursework online to streaming games and working on shared documents with classmates.
Right. What else do we need to know?

For an organisation, the cloud can save money because it does not need to buy, house and maintain its own servers or many separate software licences. Pay-as-you-go plans mean it pays only for what it uses. The service is scalable, so storage and bandwidth can be increased or reduced quickly. Storage capacity is far larger than local hard drives.
Got it. Keep going.

The provider applies software updates automatically and backs up data at regular intervals, so the organisation does not need its own backup devices or recovery procedures. Staff can access their files from anywhere and on any device, which supports home and hybrid working. If the office suffers a fire, flood or theft, the data is still safe. Using less equipment on site also reduces electricity use, which lowers the organisation's carbon footprint.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

The biggest weakness of the cloud is that it depends on the internet. If the broadband connection or the router fails, staff cannot reach their files or software. This is called downtime. Downtime can also happen if the provider has a fault or is carrying out maintenance, and the organisation cannot fix the problem itself. Some plans have a bandwidth allowance and charge extra if it is exceeded, and uploading large files can be slow.
Okay. Keep going.

Security is another concern. The data is stored by a third party, and no provider can promise that it will never be hacked. The organisation is still responsible for protecting personal data under the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. Subscription costs continue for as long as the service is used, and getting help from customer support can be slow or cost extra.
Go on.

The cloud has changed gaming for both producers and players. Producers can sell games as downloads, so they save the cost of making discs and paying shops, and can offer lower prices. Players can download a game the moment it is released. Games kept on the producer's servers are much harder to copy illegally than discs, which helps protect sales.
Right. Keep going.

The internet also gives producers a worldwide market, and they can release patches, updates and demos straight away. With cloud gaming, also called game streaming, the game runs on powerful servers and video is streamed to the player's device. This means high-quality games can be played on cheap devices without upgrading hardware. However, players need fast broadband with low latency, streaming uses a lot of data, and access is lost if the subscription ends.
Go on.

Cloud storage keeps files on high-capacity servers. Many apps save work automatically every few seconds, so a crash rarely means lost work. Files remain online until the user deletes them, and the provider keeps copies so it can recover files if a server fails, without the user needing any technical knowledge. Synchronisation means the latest version of a file appears on every device the user owns.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Sharing is easier too: instead of emailing large attachments, a user shares a link and sets permissions to decide who can view or edit. Collaborative tools such as Google Docs and Microsoft 365 let several people edit the same document at the same time, wherever they are. Version history shows who made each change and allows an earlier version to be restored, and users can be sent alerts when a document changes.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Cloud computing?
Storing data and running software on remote servers that are accessed on demand over the internet, instead of on a local computer.
Cloud storage?
Keeping files on a provider's remote servers so they can be accessed from any device with an internet connection.
Data centre?
A building containing large numbers of servers that store data and run cloud services.
Scalability?
The ability to increase or decrease storage, bandwidth or users quickly as an organisation's needs change.
Pay as you go?
A payment model where an organisation pays only for the cloud resources it actually uses.
Downtime?
A period when a service is unavailable, for example because of an internet failure or provider maintenance.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Cloud questions are usually worth a few marks each but come up often. You may be asked to define cloud computing. A two-mark definition needs two ideas: storing data or running software on remote servers, and accessing them over the internet. Benefits and risks for a business were asked in the 2023 paper, question 9 and the 2024 paper, question 2. Make each point specific and explain why it matters, for example 'needs an internet connection, so if the broadband fails staff cannot access files'. Cloud gaming was a quality of written communication question in the 2019 paper, question 7 and returned in the 2023 paper, question 9, so practise writing a balanced answer in full sentences that covers both benefits and drawbacks. Cloud storage terms appeared in the 2022 paper, question 2. Avoid vague answers such as 'it is cheaper' or 'it is easier' without saying why.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. A school's broadband fails for a morning. Why is this a problem if its files are in the cloud? Is it A, Cloud files are deleted when the internet goes down; B, Staff cannot reach the files or cloud software until the connection returns; C, The cloud provider charges a fine; D, The files become corrupted?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is B: Staff cannot reach the files or cloud software until the connection returns. Cloud services depend on an internet connection; without it there is downtime for the school.
